rounds.text: HEC Infra Projects Ltd presents a compelling case of extreme undervaluation where fundamental performance has significantly outpaced market sentiment. The company has demonstrated explosive growth, with 5-year compounded profit growth of 110% and 3-year compounded sales growth of 51% [E15, E16, E19]. Despite this, the stock trades at a modest P/E of 9.37x, which is notably lower than the sector benchmark of 14.04x [E1, E6]. The internal efficiency of the business is robust, evidenced by a superior ROE of 19.17% and ROCE of 21.4%, both of which comfortably exceed their respective sector benchmarks [E9, E10, E12]. Furthermore, management has demonstrated confidence in the company's trajectory by increasing their stake to 74.93% [E39], while operational improvements are visible through the significant reduction in debtor days from 96.2 to 55.4 [E58]. Conceded: the stock has suffered a 24% decline over the last year and currently sits below its 200-day moving average [E24, E47]. Additionally, the company does not pay a dividend, and cash conversion remains a point of concern at 0.23x [E4, E33].

Serious cash conversion risks undermine the reported profitability of HEC Infra Projects Ltd, evidenced by a cash conversion ratio of just 0.23x for March 2026 where profits far outpace actual cash generation, pointing to potential issues with receivables and accruals [E33]. Conceded: the company has delivered strong multi-year profit growth [E19, E20] and a low trailing P/E ratio [E1]. However, this profitability fails to reach shareholders in cash dividends, with a yield of 0.00% despite repeated reported profits [E4, E60]. Furthermore, financial liabilities are expanding as borrowings grew to Rs 44 Cr in March 2026 up from Rs 38 Cr a year prior [E37], alongside an inconsistent yearly and quarterly operating margin trend [E31, E32]. Institutional confidence has evaporated entirely, with domestic institutions holding 0.00% down from 8.52% in December 2023 [E40]. Technical indicators reinforce this underlying weakness, as the stock trades below both its 50-day and 200-day moving averages [E47] alongside a high annualised volatility of 61.4% [E51].

Conceded: cash conversion is 0.23x for March 2026 [E33]. However, the bear overlooks the crucial operational reality that debtor days have dramatically improved from 96.2 to 55.4 days [E58], and working capital requirements have dropped from 92.2 to 40.4 days [E59], showing collection efficiency is actively strengthening. Conceded: the dividend yield is 0.00% [E4], but the retained capital is driving extraordinary fundamental performance, led by a 5-year compounded profit growth of 110% [E19] and an ROE of 21.2% [E13] that easily eclipses the sector benchmark of 10.38% [E9]. While borrowings ticked up to Rs 44 Cr [E37], they support a robust business generating Rs 3 Cr in free cash flow [E35] with moderate leverage at 0.67x [E36], backed by promoters who actually increased their stake to 74.93% [E39]. The evaporation of domestic institutional holding [E40] simply masks a classic turnaround setup where fundamentals vastly outpace stale sentiment, evidenced by profits growing 110% while 5-year share price growth lagged at just 22% [E53]. Finally, leaning on moving averages [E47] and volatility [E51] ignores the quantitative valuation safety net: a reverse DCF shows today's price absurdly prices in -2.9% earnings growth [E44] despite a multi-year sales uptrend [E64] and rising EPS [E65].

Conceded: debtor days improved from 96.2 to 55.4 days [E58] and working capital requirements dropped from 92.2 to 40.4 days [E59]. However, this supposed collection efficiency utterly fails to translate into actual cash, as the cash conversion ratio for March 2026 languishes at an alarming 0.23x where profits are left far ahead of cash [E33]. The bull highlights extraordinary 5-year profit growth [E19] and ROCE [E12], but glosses over the reality that 10-year compounded sales growth crawls at a meager 4% [E14]. The claim that promoters increasing their stake to 74.93% [E39] overrides institutional behavior ignores the total evaporation of domestic institutional holding from 8.52% to 0.00% [E40]. While the bull dismisses moving averages [E47] and volatility [E51], the stock's 1-year return of -24% [E24] and 61.4% annualised volatility [E51] reflect genuine risk, compounded by an inconsistent operating-margin trend over the last year [E31] and two quarters [E32]. Finally, citing a reverse DCF [E44] ignores explicit bear metrics showing decelerating earnings growth [E66], zero dividend yield [E4], and rising borrowings that ticked up to Rs 44 Cr [E37].
